The EPIC Act is a rare bipartisan win against the IRA’s bureaucratic overreach. The original 9-year price control cliff for small molecule drugs was a disaster—penalizing pills that are cheaper to produce and easier for patients to access. Arbitrary timelines like this stifle innovation, diverting R&D away from critical treatments. 

Congressman Murphy’s fix aligns with real-world science: 61% of cancer drugs gain new uses post-approval. Why let D.C. price-fixing sabotage that progress? Cutting red tape for small molecules means faster generics, lower costs, and more cures—without taxpayer-funded handouts to bloated agencies.

The Veterans National Traumatic Brain Injury Treatment Act (H.R. 1336) is a critical step toward addressing the invisible wounds plaguing our veterans. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy has shown promise in clinical trials for PTSD and TBI—studies like the 2024 randomized trial published in Frontiers in Neurology demonstrated significant symptom reduction.

But here’s the catch: the bill’s pilot program relies on a donation-funded “VA HBOT Fund” instead of direct taxpayer allocation. Why outsource responsibility to charity when Congress could mandate permanent, fully-funded care? Veterans deserve more than experimental timelines and bureaucratic half-measures.

This isn’t about cutting waste—it’s about cutting through red tape to deliver proven therapies without forcing vets to rely on the generosity of strangers. Pass the bill, but fix the funding model.

The SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act of 2025 (H.R.2483) reauthorizes $505.579M annually through 2030 for overdose prevention programs, including wastewater surveillance and fentanyl detection - but the real test is whether these funds bypass bureaucratic bloat. While expanding access to recovery services is critical, Section 103's $57M annual first responder training allocation must avoid becoming another slush fund for consultants rather than frontline tools.

The bill's $38.9M/year for maternal addiction treatment (Section 201) could save lives if paired with strict outcome metrics, not just enrollment quotas. Fiscal responsibility demands clawbacks for grantees who miss 90-day performance benchmarks.

This legislation passes the sniff test only if every dollar is tracked like the opioids it aims to combat.
